name: 2001 April Storm

phenomena.details: Strong geomagnetic storm with Dst ~ −271 nT during a highly active period of Solar Cycle 23 maximum.

impacts.description: Multiple spacecraft experienced anomalies; elevated radiation belt fluxes caused increased single-event upsets and charging events.
Aurora widely visible across North America and Europe at mid-latitudes.
HF radio disruptions on high-latitude routes; polar cap absorption events affected transpolar aviation communications.

papers.title: Solar and interplanetary sources of major geomagnetic storms ( Dst ≤ −100 nT) during 1996–2005
papers.authors: Zhang, J., Richardson, I. G., Webb, D. F., et al.
papers.journal: Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics
papers.keyFinding: Catalogue of solar and interplanetary sources of all Dst ≤ −100 nT storms 1996–2005, identifying the source of the April 2001 storm.

summary: The April 2001 storm (Dst ~ −271 nT), driven by an X2.3 flare from AR 9415, was part of an unusually active period during Solar Cycle 23 maximum that produced multiple intense geomagnetic storms in rapid succession.
description: On April 11, 2001, just weeks after the March 2001 storm, another intense geomagnetic storm struck Earth, driven by an X2.3 flare from AR 9415 and an associated fast halo CME (~1200 km/s). The storm reached Dst ~ −271 nT, making it another strong event in what was proving to be an exceptionally active period during Solar Cycle 23's maximum. The storm caused satellite anomalies, HF radio disruptions, and aurora visible at mid-latitudes. The rapid succession of intense storms during this period stressed the space weather forecasting community and demonstrated how clustered solar activity can create compound space weather impacts.
